strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing the gap between static medical benchmarks and dynamic clinical inquiry, effectively illustrated with compelling motivating example (Figure 1)
Comprehensive framework design with thoughtful two-tiered reward architecture that separately optimizes soft skills (communication) and hard skills (diagnosis)
Strong empirical results: 8B model outperforms Baichuan-M2-32B (4× parameters), competitive with GPT-4.1, and strong human evaluation across all metrics
Thorough experimental evaluation across multiple benchmarks (HealthBench, MAQuE, MedQA, MMLU) with detailed ablations and scaling studies
Excellent reproducibility with extensive implementation details, hyperparameters, and system prompts in appendices
Good parameter efficiency demonstration and maintained foundational knowledge on static QA tasks
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily combines existing components (GRPO, multi-agent simulation, experience repositories) without significant innovation in individual methods
Evaluation methodology concerns: heavy reliance on LLM-based evaluation (GPT-4.1 as judge) and circular dependency of using Qwen3-8B as policy model, patient agent, and reward model simultaneously
Patient agent fidelity issues: Qwen3-8B simulation may lack realism, mitigation strategies are heuristic, and no quantitative adherence metrics reported beyond rule-based checks
Reward function design relies on many ad-hoc hyperparameters (Table 4) with insufficient justification; penalty values in Eq. 2 and weights unexplained, no sensitivity analysis
Modest ablation improvements suggest individual components contribute less than claimed (10% drop w/o process reward, 13% w/o experience); no ablation on GRPO algorithm itself
Potential data leakage from experience repository where high-reward training trajectories may overlap with test cases
Large performance degradation on harder cases (36.29→18.73 from Main to Hard dataset) raises generalization concerns
Human evaluation lacks inter-annotator agreement metrics, limited to 5 annotators, and no statistical significance testing
Overclaimed contributions (e.g., 'mastering clinical inquiry' when 10-point gap exists between easy/hard benchmarks)
Limited technical novelty in individual components; GRPO framework and experience retrieval are standard techniques

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing gap between static QA and dynamic clinical reasoning
Comprehensive experimental infrastructure with multiple benchmarks (HealthBench, MAQuE, MedQA, MMLU) and diverse baselines
Thoughtful framework design integrating process rewards (soft skills) and outcome rewards (hard skills) with hierarchical veto system
Extensive implementation details and ablation studies supporting reproducibility efforts
Illustrative case study (Table 9) effectively demonstrating failure modes of existing models on challenging scenarios
weaknesses: Critical circular evaluation bias: model trained with Qwen3-8B reward function then evaluated using similar LLM judges, creating unfair advantage over models like GPT-4.1 not optimized for those evaluators—undermines central claims of surpassing proprietary models

Extraordinary claims (8B model surpasses GPT-4.1, Claude Sonnet 4) lack sufficient evidence: modest performance gaps (5-10 points) without statistical significance testing or confidence intervals; actually loses to larger models on harder cases (18.73 vs 23.68 on HealthBench Hard)

All evaluation relies on LLM judges with no ground truth validation; benchmarks (HealthBench, MAQuE from 2025) have unvalidated reliability; human evaluation uses only 5 non-expert annotators with no inter-rater reliability reported

Synthetic training environment with same model family (Qwen3-8B) for both patient simulation and evaluation raises transfer concerns; no evaluation on real clinical conversations or genuine human interaction

Limited technical novelty: GRPO is existing method (Shao et al. 2024); multi-objective RL with weighted combining is standard; multi-stage retrieval is reasonable but conventional; main contribution is applying existing techniques to medical domain, not methodological innovation

Ablation studies lack rigor: 'w/o Experience' still uses rewards and RL training, not isolating experience repository's contribution; no comparison with simpler SFT baseline on same 100k dialogues; missing ablations on different RL algorithms, reward designs, and individual reward dimensions

Hyperparameter choices lack justification: reward weights (wsafety=1.0 to whumility=0.5) and veto thresholds appear arbitrary with no sensitivity analysis; training uses single epoch without validation curves

Reproducibility gaps: model weights unavailable, training code not mentioned, 100k dialogue dataset not available, experience repository not available, incomplete abstract reference; independent verification impossible

Parameter efficiency claims unsubstantiated: hidden computational cost of 100k training interactions with multiple LLM calls (patient agent, reward model, embedding model, reranker) not disclosed; total FLOPs and wall-clock time not reported
Data contamination risk: training on KaMed, then evaluating on 2025 benchmarks; no explicit statement that evaluation data was held-out during training

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Clear distinction between static medical QA and dynamic clinical inquiry, effectively demonstrated through the hemoptysis example
Comprehensive framework design: Two-tiered reward architecture with hierarchical veto system, multi-stage experience retrieval, and three-principle approach are thoughtfully engineered
Strong empirical results: Outperforms proprietary models (GPT-4.1, Grok-4, Claude Sonnet 4) and substantially outperforms larger open-source models (8B vs 32B/70B) on HealthBench and MAQuE

Thorough empirical validation: Extensive baseline comparisons, proper human evaluation (5 annotators), ablation studies confirming component importance, and scaling studies showing systematic improvements
Excellent reproducibility: Comprehensive appendices with implementation details, hyperparameters, system prompts, and methodological descriptions enabling reproduction
Knowledge retention: Results on MedQA (83.5%) and MMLU (85%) confirm that specialized training doesn't degrade foundational knowledge
Well-organized presentation: Clear narrative structure, compelling figures (especially Figure 1), and appropriate use of tables and appendices
weaknesses: Evaluator circularity: The same Qwen3-8B model serves as both the reward model during RL training and the Consultation Evaluator, creating potential bias in reported results despite human spot-checking claims

Limited algorithmic novelty: Framework primarily combines existing techniques (GRPO from Shao et al. 2024, standard experience replay, multi-agent RL). Main novelty is in application rather than methodology
Single base model: All experiments use Qwen3-8B. Generalization to other base models (Llama, Mistral, etc.) unclear, limiting claims about framework effectiveness
Missing statistical rigor: No confidence intervals, significance tests, or inter-evaluator agreement metrics reported. Human evaluation with only 5 annotators lacks statistical validation
Incomplete failure analysis: Limited discussion of failure modes. HealthBench Hard gap (18.73 vs Baichuan-M2-32B's 23.68) not explained. Case studies only show success/failure contrasts
Limited generalization testing: English-only evaluation acknowledged. No multilingual or multi-domain testing despite claims about dynamic inquiry applicability
Reward function design justification: Specific weights in Table 4 and threshold values (ε=0, β_std for dynamic threshold) lack principled justification. Sensitivity analysis absent
Unfair baseline comparisons: Compared open-source models not specifically trained for multi-turn dialogue, making it unclear if improvements come from the framework or from dialogue-specific training

strengths: Well-motivated problem identification addressing gap between static QA benchmarks and dynamic clinical practice with clear principle-based framework
Thoughtful system design including hierarchical veto system for safety, two-tiered rewards for soft/hard skills, and multi-stage experience retrieval
Strong empirical results demonstrating parameter efficiency (8B model competitive with 32B+ models) across two benchmarks with substantial improvements (e.g., +25.05 communication quality)
Comprehensive evaluation including diverse baselines, multiple metrics, extensive ablation studies, and both automated and human evaluation
Excellent reproducibility with detailed implementation specifications, promised code release, and extensive appendices
Safety-conscious framing acknowledging limitations and research-only status
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core components (GRPO, LLM rewards, multi-agent simulation) are existing techniques; contribution is primarily application-focused combination rather than fundamental innovation
Evaluation reliability concerns: HealthBench/MAQuE use LLM judges (GPT-4.1) where medical hallucinations are not well-controlled; cross-validator study shows only moderate agreement (ρ>0.24)
Insufficient human evaluation: only 2 physicians on 80 trajectories for clinical competence; no inter-rater reliability statistics; potential evaluator bias not addressed
Experimental fairness issues: unclear if all baseline models received identical prompting; proprietary models evaluated via APIs vs. open-source via vLLM; uncontrolled for temperature settings
Training data advantage: paper trains on 100k task-specific simulated dialogues; unclear if improvements reflect reasoning gains vs. domain-specific overfitting
Experience repository design issues: novelty/reward thresholds appear ad-hoc with no sensitivity analysis; Table 9 suggests in-context learning may drive gains more than learned policy

Lack of statistical rigor: no confidence intervals or significance testing on main results; ablation improvements lack uncertainty quantification; small sample sizes for human evaluation not acknowledged
Generalization concerns: evaluation restricted to English, public benchmarks; no analysis across patient demographics, condition types, or truly out-of-distribution scenarios
Base model bias: both policy and reward model are Qwen3-8B, potentially optimizing toward same family; limited transferability validation (only one alternative base model tested)
Overstated claims: 'mastering clinical inquiry' and 'outperforms proprietary models' need qualification; advantage claims not nuanced about evaluation methodology limitations

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing the gap between static medical knowledge and dynamic clinical practice
Comprehensive experimental framework with multiple benchmarks (HealthBench, MAQuE, MedQA, MMLU) and extensive ablations
Strong engineering execution combining multiple components coherently with thoughtful design (e.g., hierarchical veto system)
Parameter efficiency: competitive performance with 8B model versus larger baselines
Commitment to reproducibility with detailed implementation details and promise of code/weight release
Extensive human evaluation combining patient perspectives and physician expertise
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (GRPO, experience retrieval, multi-agent simulation, hierarchical rewards) without introducing novel methods or principles
Evaluation entirely on synthetic benchmarks with LLM-based scoring (Qwen3-8B); Spearman correlation with human experts is weak (ρ > 0.24), raising validity concerns
Simulated patient agent behavior is unvalidated against real patients; 13.82% dialogue rejection rate suggests fragility; could introduce systematic training biases
No real clinical validation or demonstration of generalization to actual clinical practice; system explicitly stated as unsuitable for deployment
Reward model reliability questionable: uses another LLM (Qwen3-8B) with limited spot-checking (50 samples/day) and only 2 physicians for human validation
Missing statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, significance tests, or error bars on main results; human evaluation sample too small (2 experts, 5 annotators)

Overclaimed contributions: title 'mastering clinical inquiry' overstates incremental benchmark improvements; 'Experiential Agentic RL' branded but is standard multi-agent RL plus off-the-shelf experience retrieval
Training data contaminated by GPT-4.1 annotation (CoT format), introducing implicit bias; comparison with GPT-4.1 less meaningful as a result
Limited generalization evidence: framework transferability shown only on Llama-3.1; hyperparameters appear tuned to Qwen3-8B; no multilingual evaluation
Computational accessibility poor: requires 7× A100-80GB GPUs; 20.38% training overhead; reproducibility limited despite detailed documentation
Incomplete comparisons: 8B vs. GPT-4.1 not equivalent baselines; missing ablations showing why GRPO theoretically outperforms PPO; no few-shot baseline
Documented failure modes (Appendix F.2) show system still makes dangerous clinical recommendations despite proposed mitigations

strengths: Clear and important problem: Well-motivated gap between static QA performance and dynamic multi-turn clinical consultation capabilities
Comprehensive technical framework: Elegant integration of multi-agent environment, two-tiered reward system, and sophisticated experience retrieval with 3-stage pipeline
Strong empirical results: 8B model outperforms larger open-source models (32B-70B) and proprietary models like GPT-4.1 with substantial margins on HealthBench and MAQuE
Thorough experimental validation: Appropriate algorithmic ablations, scaling studies, multiple human evaluation cohorts, and cross-evaluator validation demonstrating consistency
Excellent reproducibility: Complete implementation details, full system prompts, hyperparameters, and clear description of 100k simulated dialogues; code/weights promised for release
Thoughtful analysis and honesty: Insightful failure mode analysis, explicit discussion of reward hacking mitigation, and candid acknowledgment of limitations and safety concerns
Clear presentation and organization: Well-written with effective figures, logical flow, and comprehensive appendices supporting main claims
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: GRPO from existing work, multi-agent simulations established, two-tiered rewards not new; primary contribution is application rather than novel techniques

Evaluation methodology concerns: Heavy reliance on LLM judge (Qwen3-8B); clinical expert evaluation limited to 2 physicians on 80 cases with no inter-rater reliability reported; experience utility evaluated on only 30 cases

Simulated patient agent design limitations: Using Qwen3-8B as patient may introduce systematic biases; potential gap between simulation and real patient interactions; 13.82% rejection rate impact not fully analyzed

Safety concerns despite safeguards: 0.80% safety violation rate remains concerning for clinical deployment; failure cases show agent can miss critical checks (missed medications, red flags); marketing language may oversell readiness

Limited baseline comparisons: Missing direct comparisons with other medical RL approaches beyond DoctorAgent-RL; no comparison with concurrent work like Agent Hospital; primarily compares against general LLMs rather than specialized medical agents

Generalization and scaling questions: Extensive testing only on 8B base model; limited transferability evidence (only Llama-3.1-8B); unclear how approach scales to larger models or other architectures; English-only evaluation

Ad-hoc design choices: Experience retrieval hyperparameters (α, β_std, τ_novelty, τ_reward) lack principled justification or sensitivity analysis; reward weights in Table 6 appear manually tuned without thorough ablation

Incomplete ablation analysis: Component contributions shown but interaction effects not fully explored; unclear which specific elements (RL training vs. experience retrieval vs. reward design) drive superiority over GPT-4.1
